rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı links Qāf’s opening letter and Quran oath, the disbelievers’ amazement, and the closing command to remind with the Quran to Sad’s frame; Sad stresses tawhid, while Qāf attends to resurrection.
rows.anchor: Bu sûre ile Sâd Sûresi’nin başlayışında ziyade bir benzeyiş vardır.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāf is written as a letter but read by its name, which also names the sura; proposals include Qāf Mountain or a symbolic or explicit imperative, but the letter is ultimately among the ambiguous openings whose interpretation God knows.
rows.anchor: Yazılışta harf, okunuşta “kāf” isim tarzındadır. Zahir olan harfin ismi, bundan da bu sûrenin ismidir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı classifies the opening letter among the mutashabihat and says its interpretation is known by God, leaving the mountain and imperative readings unestablished.
rows.anchor: Doğrusu diğerleri gibi bu da müteşâbihâttandır. Tevilini Allah bilir.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi explains the disconnected letters at sura openings as alerts that awaken listeners’ attention so they will hear the Quran being recited.
rows.anchor: Fahreddin Râzî burada evvelâ şu ihtarâtta bulunmuştur:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı reports Razi’s comparison of letter-recitation to worship: some bodily and inward rites are intelligible while others depend only on transmitted revelation; disconnected letters can likewise be recited in pure obedience without ordinary propositional meaning.
rows.anchor: ibadetin kalb ile olanı, lisan ile olanı, bedenin zâhirdeki cevârihi ile olanı vardır.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says the oath by letters confers honor on them: letters are the basis of noble speech and the means by which knowledge and definition are expressed.
rows.anchor: Bu harflere yemin edilmiş bulunuyor, muksemun bih mevkiindedirler, hâlbuki Allah teâlâ’nın tîn ve zeytuna kasemi onlara şeref vermek olduğu gibi, marifetin delîli ve târifin âleti olan şerefli kelâmın aslı olan harflere kasemi de onların ayrıca bir şerefi hâiz olduklarını evleviyetle ifade eder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı reports Razi’s count: oaths range from one to five objects or letters; only the sun oath exceeds five objects, no oath uses more than five letters, and longer root-forms are considered cumbersome, especially when their meaning is obscure.
rows.anchor: 1. Allah teâlâ’dan kasem ya وَالْعَصْرِ، وَالنَّجْمِ gibi bir şeye ve صٓ، قٓ، نٓ gibi bir harfe vâki‘olmuştur

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi observes that familiar objects sworn by take the oath particle waw, whereas letter-oaths omit it, since using one letter as the instrument introducing an oath on another would upset their equality.
rows.anchor: Ma‘hud şeylere kasemde kasem harfi olan vâv zikredilmiş وَالطُّورِ، وَالنَّجْمِ، وَالشَّمْسِ denilmiş, lâkin harflere kasemde kasem harfi zikredilmemiştir.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi contrasts oaths on objects, whose excellence lies in their composition rather than their basic matter, with oaths on isolated letters; combined letters denote meanings, so uncombined letters are nobler than meaningless compounds.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ, تِين، طُور gibi eşyâya kasem etmiş, onların asılları olan cevher-i ferdlere, basit maddelerine

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi counts letter-oaths in 28 suras and object-oaths in 14; letter-oaths occur only at openings, where an understood subject can follow an obscure letter, while object-oaths can appear elsewhere.
rows.anchor: yirmi sekiz sûrededir. Adetleri harflerin adedince olan eşyâya kasem ise

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi says letter-oaths occur across both Quranic halves and all seven sections because the Quranic miracle is expressed through letters; oaths on counted objects are mostly confined to the latter half.
rows.anchor: Harflere kasem, Kur’ân’ın iki nısfının ikisinde de hatta yedi kısmında da vardır

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi notes that letter-oaths are often followed by “Quran,” “Book,” or “revelation,” since the Quran is a miracle formed from letters and appears throughout the Quran, unlike the oaths on enumerated objects.
rows.anchor: Zira ekseriya harflere kasemden sonra “Kur’an” veya “kitab” veya “tenzil” zikredilmiş, يٰسٓ وَالْقُرْاٰنِ الْحَك۪يمِ، الٓـمٓ تَنْز۪يلُ الْكِتَابِ، الٓمٓ ذٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ buyurulmuştur.

rows.speaker: Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Razi rejects identifying this Qāf with the world-encircling mountain: the pause, missing oath particle, spelling ق rather than قاف, and Ibn Abbas’s report do not establish that referent here.
rows.anchor: Bundan sonra Râzî “Kāf”a mahsus mebâhisten olmak üzere şunu da ilâve eder: “Kāf Arz’ı muhit olan bir dağdır ki semânın etrafı onun üzerindedir denilmiş, bu kavil, vücûh ile zayıftır:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı clarifies that Razi does not deny the reports of Qāf Mountain; he considers using them to interpret this opening weak.
rows.anchor: Demek ki Râzî esas itibariyle Kaf dağı diye söylenegelen rivayeti inkâr etmiyor, burada onunla tefsiri zayıf buluyor.

rows.speaker: Karâfî
rows.claim: Al-Qarafi holds that Qāf Mountain does not exist and that belief in an unproven thing is impermissible; Ibn Hajar al-Haytami objects by adducing the transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: Karâfî, Kaf Dağı’nın vücûdu olmadığına zâhib olmuş

rows.speaker: İbn Hacer Heytemî
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami objects to al-Qarafi’s denial by citing reports about Qāf Mountain.
rows.anchor: İbn Hacer Heytemî de vârid olan rivayetleri ileri sürerek ona bazı itirazda bulunmuştur.

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi sides with al-Qarafi, arguing from sensory observation that traversing the earth and sea to the polar regions revealed no such mountain.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî bunları hikâye ettikten sonra “ben de” diyor, “Karâfî’nin dediği gibi his şehadetiyle bu dağın vücûdu olmadığına zâhib oluyorum.

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi says questioning the authenticity of reports whose narrators insist on their soundness is less harmful than contradicting sensory evidence; he distinguishes this from denying existence merely because something was not found.
rows.anchor: onların sıhhatine ta‘n etmek hissi tekzib etmekten ehvendir.

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi argues that earthquakes need no mountain to explain them: pressure from vapors trying to escape the solid earth causes them, so denying the mountain is no mere argument from failure to find it.
rows.anchor: Zelzele işinin de öyle bir dağa tevakkufu yoktur, çünkü zelzeleler Arz’ın salâbetiyle beraber çıkmak isteyen buharların tazyîkindendir.

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi calls denial of Qāf Mountain obstinate for anyone with even a little fairness.
rows.anchor: Ve biraz insaf damarı olanlar nazarında bunu inkâr etmek mükâberedir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı considers Razi more judicious and prefers finding a sound interpretation for the reports to rejecting them; he notes that no report about Qāf is traced back to the Prophet, though a widespread scholarly view exists.
rows.anchor: Bizce insaf rivayetleri tekzib etmekte değil, bir mahmil-i sahih bulmaktadır.

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: According to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abbas says God placed an encircling sea behind the earth, then created Qāf Mountain behind it with the lowest heaven hanging over it.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas şöyle demiştir: “Allah teâlâ bu Arz’ın arkasından onu muhît bir deniz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı interprets the report’s encompassing sea and Qāf as the atmosphere: the ocean surrounds the earth, the atmosphere surrounds the ocean, and the lowest heaven rests on the atmosphere; the emerald color represents its greenish appearance.
rows.anchor: Demek ki Kaf Arz’ı kaplamış olan bahr-ı muhîti muhîttir. Bu ifadeye göre Kaf Dağı denilen şey küre-i nesîm olmuş olur.

rows.speaker: Abdullah b. Büreyde
rows.claim: Reports from Abdullah b. Burayda describe Qāf as an emerald mountain encircling the world with the edges of heaven above it; Elmalılı reads the emerald as a rhetorical image for the atmosphere’s color.
rows.anchor: İbn Münzir’in, Ebu’ş-Şeyh’in, Hâkim’in, İbn Merdûye’nin Abdullah b. Büreyde’den rivayetlerinde “Kaf, dünyayı muhît zümrüdden bir dağdır ki semânın etekleri onun üzerindedir”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says calling it a mountain may refer to its spherical shape, height above the horizon and grandeur, or its role as a source and reservoir.
rows.anchor: Buna “dağ” tâbir olunması da şekl-i kürevîsi ile fevka’l-ufuk irtifâ‘ve azameti haysiyetinden yahut bir menba‘ve mahzen olması nokta-i nazarından olmak gerektir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports compiled by Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Abu al-Shaykh say Qāf encompasses the whole world, its roots reach into earth, and earthquakes result from their movement.
rows.anchor: Kaf yalnız Arz’ı değil, âlemi muhît olmak üzere de nakledilmiş ve damarları Arz’ın içine kadar indiği

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qāf reports remind Elmalılı of Greek “chaos” (kao), an ancient idea of primordial mixed matter as the source of everything; since the reports are not Prophetic, he allows them as an old widespread theory but not as a basis for exegesis.
rows.anchor: Bu noktaya gelince “Kaf” kelimesi bize eski Yunânîlerde dahi mâruf olan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı prefers reading the letter Qāf as an ambiguous allusion to divine power over interpreting it through Qāf Mountain as the realm of possibility.
rows.anchor: ق harfini müteşâbih olarak kudretullâha bir remiz telakkī etmek Kaf Dağı denilen imkân âlemiyle tefsir etmekten daha münâsib olur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Majīd means possessing majesty, expansive generosity, great honor, and glory; “Majestic Quran” may mean the Quran nobler than all books or one that ennobles those who know and practice its meaning.
rows.anchor: “Mecîd”, mecd sahibi, mecd geniş kerem ile alâkadar büyük şeref ve şandır.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw can mark an oath or coordinate an oath; the oath’s response is omitted and supplied by context: the Prophet came as a warner, but his people were astonished that one of their own warned them.
rows.anchor: “Vav” kasem yahut kaseme atıf içindir. Kāf ile şanlı Kur’ân’a kasem edilmiştir. Kasemin cevâbı mâba‘di karînesiyle mahzuftur, yani sen münzirsin inzar için geldin

words: بَلْ عَجِبُوٓا۟ أَن جَآءَهُم مُّنذِرٌۭ مِّنْهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They rejected the warning because a prophet from their own kind astonished them; an outsider warning them might seem unnatural, but one of their own was not an extraordinary occurrence.
rows.anchor: Hâlbuki insanlara kendi hâriçlerinden gelen bir münzir, gayr-i tabî‘î ve şâyân-ı taaccüb görülse bile yine kendilerinden bir münzir gelmesi görülmedik bir şey değil idi.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one reading, the next clause explains their amazement and makes their disbelief explicit: the particle fa is explanatory and “this” points to the Prophet’s warning.
rows.anchor: Birisi taaccüblerini tefsir ve taaccüb noktasını tafsil ile küfürlerini tasrihtir. Bu surette فا tefsir, هذا Peygamber’in inzârına işarettir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the other reading, after marveling at the Prophet’s mission they also marvel at resurrection: fa coordinates the clauses, and “this” refers ambiguously to their question about being raised after death.
rows.anchor: İkincisi Peygamber’in bi‘setine taaccübden sonra âhirette ba‘se taaccüblerini beyandır. Bu surette فا atıf هذا mübhem olarak şu söze işaret olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase calls resurrection after death a distant return, remote from reason or custom; “ircāʿ” can also mean a reply or response.
rows.anchor: ba‘îd bir ircâ‘akıldan veya âdetten uzak olan bir iade, bir döndürüş yahut bir cevaptır.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrection seems remote only because people cannot fully know a person’s reality and components; if all identity-making secrets were known, recreating the dead would not seem difficult.
rows.anchor: Yani onun uzak zannedilmesi bir insanın hakikati ve eczâsının tafsîlâtı tamamıyla bilinemediği için cehaletten neş’et eder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı asks whether what remains or disappears as a person decays is spirit, body, bodily matter, or a determinate relation among similar components that conveys life and identity; God knows every fine detail and property thought lost.
rows.anchor: Rûh mudur, beden midir? Bedenin maddesi ve eczâsı mıdır, yoksa mütemâsil eczâ arasında hayâtı ve ayniyeti ifade eden bir nisbet-i muayyene ve mahsûsası mıdır? Allah hepsini bilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preserved book is immutable and records everything, particular and universal, including every detail of human deeds; it makes divine knowledge manifest and secure in the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: Ve nezdimizde mahfuz, değişmez, bozulmaz bir kitap vardır, hepsi onda mazbuttur. Cüz’î ve küllî hiçbir şeyi kaçırmaz, hatta onların amellerini de bütün tafsîlâtıyla hıfzetmektedir.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı also reads the preserved record as an expression of the law of transformation and conservation: once a person’s dispersed properties remain known and preserved, reconstituting that person is no distant return for God.
rows.anchor: Bunu tehavvül ve tehaffuz kanununun bir ifadesi olarak da mülâhaza edebiliriz.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers rejected the truth as soon as it came, thereby denying the knowledge of their Creator and the revealed book and prophet; they now waver in a turbulent state, calling the Prophet a magician, soothsayer, or poet and despairing of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: Fakat onlar hakkı kendilerine geldiği anda

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı reads the description of their turmoil as leading into the following proof of God’s knowledge and power to revive, which is meant to dispel their confusion.
rows.anchor: Buna karşı Allah teâlâ’nın ilmini ve ihyâya kudretini isbat ile ıztırâbı def‘siyâkında buyuruluyor ki:
